slots.practicalActivity: Sign up for (or log into) a real AWS Free Tier account, open the Management Console, and use the top services search to find and open S3, Lambda, and Redshift one at a time without configuring anything, confirming for yourself that "AWS" is a catalog of 200+ separate products rather than one dashboard.
slots.deliverable: A short note confirming you opened the AWS Console and located S3, Lambda, and Redshift via services search, with one sentence on which Azure service (if any) you'd have assumed each one directly replaces.

lessons.title: AWS Global Infrastructure: Regions & Availability Zones

slots.practicalActivity: In the AWS Console, use the Region selector in the top-right to switch between two real Regions (e.g. us-east-1 and eu-west-1) and note how a service's resource list (try EC2) changes between them, then open the account menu to find your 12-digit Account ID, confirming Regions and account identity are two separate things.
slots.deliverable: A written note naming the two Regions you switched between, what changed in the console each time, and your own AWS Account ID.

slots.practicalActivity: Open your account's Billing and Organizations pages (even on a single standalone account) to see where multi-account structure would live, then write a shared-responsibility table for S3 listing what AWS manages (durability, hardware, data center security) versus what you manage (bucket policies, encryption choices, who has access).
slots.deliverable: A written shared-responsibility table for S3 splitting AWS's responsibilities from yours.

slots.practicalActivity: In the IAM console, create a real IAM user named etl-test-user (programmatic access only, no console password), create a group named Data-Engineers, attach the AWS-managed AmazonS3ReadOnlyAccess policy to the group, and add the user to it; then create an IAM role trusted by the Lambda service to see the trust-policy screen roles use that users don't.
slots.deliverable: A real IAM user inside a real IAM group with an attached managed policy, plus one IAM role created for Lambda, both visible in the IAM console's Users, Groups, and Roles lists.

slots.practicalActivity: Walk the full EC2 launch wizard for a free-tier-eligible t2.micro/t3.micro instance (launching it, or stopping just before the final Launch click if you want to avoid any charge) to see the AMI, instance type, and security group choices, then create a real S3 bucket with a globally unique name and upload one small file to it.
slots.deliverable: A real S3 bucket containing one uploaded file, plus a written note on the three choices (AMI, instance type, security group) the EC2 launch wizard asked for.

slots.practicalActivity: In the VPC console, open your account's default VPC and inspect its CIDR block, its subnets (check each one's route table to tell public from private), and its default security group's inbound rules.
slots.deliverable: A written note listing your default VPC's CIDR block, how many subnets are public vs. private, and the default security group's inbound rule.

slots.practicalActivity: Open AWS Pricing Calculator and build a real estimate for a small pipeline (one S3 bucket, one small EC2 instance, one Lambda function with a modest monthly invocation count), then open Cost Explorer and AWS Budgets and create a real $5/month budget alert on your own account.
slots.deliverable: A saved Pricing Calculator estimate for a 3-service pipeline, plus a real $5 monthly budget alert configured in your AWS account's Budgets.

lessons.title: Users, Groups & Roles
lessons.chapterTitle: IAM Deep Dive for Data Engineers

slots.practicalActivity: Create a second IAM role, this time trusted by Amazon EC2 instead of Lambda, attach the AmazonS3ReadOnlyAccess managed policy to it, and compare its trust-policy JSON (who can assume it) against the Lambda role's trust policy from the IAM Basics lab, identifying exactly what's different.
slots.deliverable: A real EC2 IAM role with an attached policy, plus a written comparison of its trust-policy JSON against the earlier Lambda role's.

lessons.title: Policies & Permissions
lessons.chapterTitle: IAM Deep Dive for Data Engineers

slots.practicalActivity: Write a custom JSON policy granting only s3:GetObject and s3:PutObject on one specific bucket ARN (not *), attach it to etl-test-user, then use the IAM Policy Simulator to confirm an s3:DeleteObject call on that same bucket is correctly denied.
slots.deliverable: A custom least-privilege JSON policy attached to a real IAM identity, plus a Policy Simulator result confirming s3:DeleteObject is denied while s3:GetObject/s3:PutObject are allowed.

lessons.title: Least Privilege for Data Pipelines
lessons.chapterTitle: IAM Deep Dive for Data Engineers

lessons.title: Cross-Service Access Patterns
lessons.chapterTitle: IAM Deep Dive for Data Engineers

slots.practicalActivity: Rewrite your policy to scope it to one prefix inside the bucket (e.g. arn:aws:s3:::your-bucket/raw/*) instead of the whole bucket, following the ingestion-Lambda/Glue-job pattern from the lesson, then sketch in a doc a real cross-service access pattern — a Lambda execution role that can read one S3 prefix and write to one DynamoDB table — writing out the two specific resource ARNs it would need scoped access to.
slots.deliverable: A prefix-scoped IAM policy (not bucket-wide) verified in the Policy Simulator, plus a written cross-service access design naming the two specific resource ARNs one Lambda execution role would need.

slots.practicalActivity: Install the AWS CLI, run aws configure with a real access key pair for etl-test-user, then run aws s3 ls, create a test bucket with aws s3 mb, and upload a small file to it with aws s3 cp.
slots.deliverable: A working AWS CLI configured against your own account, with terminal output showing a successful aws s3 ls, a newly created bucket, and one uploaded file.

slots.practicalActivity: Install boto3 (pip install boto3) and write a short Python script that creates an S3 client, lists your account's buckets, and uploads one local file to the bucket created in the previous slot, using the same credentials aws configure already set up.
slots.deliverable: A working Python script using boto3 that lists your real S3 buckets and successfully uploads one file, with its console output captured.

slots.practicalActivity: Run the lesson's full round trip for real: aws s3 mb to create a uniquely named bucket, aws s3 cp to upload a text file, aws s3 ls and aws s3 cp <path> - to verify its contents from the terminal, then aws s3 rm followed by aws s3 rb to delete the object and the bucket, confirming cleanup so nothing keeps billing.
slots.deliverable: Terminal output showing the full mb -> cp -> ls/verify -> rm -> rb round trip completed successfully against a real AWS account.

slots.practicalActivity: Open the official AWS Certified Data Engineer – Associate exam guide and map each of its stated exam domains against this course's four chapters, writing one sentence per domain on whether this course covered it, the AWS Data Engineering course ahead will cover it, or it's genuinely out of scope for this path.
slots.deliverable: A written domain-by-domain mapping of the AWS Certified Data Engineer – Associate exam guide against this course's four chapters, closing out the course.

monthlyMilestoneContribution: After finishing this course, a student can navigate the AWS Console and account structure, create and scope real IAM users, roles, and least-privilege policies, and operate AWS from the CLI and SDK — the account, identity, and tooling foundation every later AWS Data Engineering lab in this path assumes is already in place.
